claims.text: The starting AlCoCrFeNi-based eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar microstructure containing FCC and B2 phases.
Low-temperature aging can induce coherent nanoscale L12 precipitates in the FCC regions of this eutectic alloy.
The aging treatment will produce a uniform L12 population specifically along lamellar colony interfaces as well as in intralamellar regions.
Annealing at approximately 600 °C for 1–2 hours is sufficient to generate the proposed precipitate structure.
The treatment should be conducted under an inert atmosphere and followed by controlled cooling.
The relevant mechanical test is quasi-static uniaxial tension at room temperature and a strain rate near 10^-3 s^-1.
Tight control of aging time and temperature, monitored by in-situ TEM or APT, will ensure a uniform precipitate distribution.
Nanoscale L12 precipitates act as controlled obstacles to dislocation motion.
The L12 precipitates act as dislocation sinks and promote more uniform dislocation motion.
L12 precipitates prevent excessive dislocation pile-ups at lamellar interfaces.
Dislocation pile-ups at lamellar interfaces cause local stress concentrations, microcrack initiation, and catastrophic damage in the starting alloy.
Coherency of the L12 precipitates maintains strong interphase bonding and facilitates effective load transfer.
L12 precipitation can increase the alloy's yield strength through precipitate–dislocation interactions.
After aging, yield strength will be retained or modestly increased to approximately 900–1074 MPa.
After aging, tensile elongation may exceed 20%, representing an increase over the untreated material.
The intervention will enhance overall work hardening.
The untreated starting alloy has approximately 13% tensile elongation and a yield strength of approximately 780–990 MPa under quasi-static loading.
The effectiveness of the intervention at high strain rates or elevated temperatures has not been established.
A nonuniform or coarsened precipitate distribution may compromise ductility or promote localized embrittlement.
Failure of uniformly L12-precipitated samples to improve ductility relative to an untreated control would falsify the proposed ductility mechanism.

contradictions.description: The mechanism predicts that a uniform precipitate distribution suppresses pile-ups and microcracking, but the falsification rule also treats failure of nonuniform precipitates to correlate with reduced microcracking as falsifying. That latter result is compatible with, rather than contrary to, the proposed need for uniformity.
